The Terms of Trade

Who writes the rules of world trade, who carries the goods, who sets the prices, and who keeps the money between the person who makes a thing and the person who buys it. One story, told on the map from the top of the system down.

About This Map
Method and Sources
On the Map

About This Map

Nearly everything a person eats, wears or uses has crossed a border on its way to them. This map asks who is paid along that journey, who writes the rules for it, and why the people who grow and make the goods receive so little of the price.

The phrase terms of trade comes from economics. It means the rate at which what a country sells abroad exchanges for what it buys: how many sacks of coffee it takes to pay for one tractor. The map uses the phrase in that sense and in a wider one. It looks at who sets the terms on which trade takes place at all. Who decides which tariffs a country may charge? Who lends the money, and in whose currency? Who owns the ships, the trading houses and the brands? Who collects the difference between seven cents paid to a cocoa farmer and a dollar paid for chocolate?

One Story, Told From the Top Down

The map's central feature is one story, arranged in 7 parts and 22 chapters. Part 1 begins with how trade works: what crosses a border, how it is paid for, and what follows when a government raises or lowers a tariff, a subsidy or another barrier. It then gives the history of how the world's trade routes were first laid, and follows three everyday products from the maker to the shop to see how the price is divided. Part 2 examines the organisations that write the rules: the World Trade Organization, the lenders in Washington, the hundreds of separate trade deals and the private tribunals attached to them. Part 3 looks at the money trade is paid in. Part 4 follows the trading houses and shipping lines that move the goods. Part 5 turns to how production is divided between countries and where the profit is recorded. Part 6 follows what comes back to poorer countries in return, which is imported food and exported waste. Part 7 closes the loop with the theory that is taught to justify the arrangement and the owners who collect its earnings.

The order matters. A farmer's price is easier to understand once the trading house that buys the crop has been introduced, and the trading house is easier to understand once the rules and the money above it are visible. Each chapter therefore follows from the layer above it. The story is not an argument against people in different places exchanging things with each other, which they have always done. It is an account of who controls the system through which that exchange now passes, and who is paid.

To follow the story in order, press Play the Story. You can also select any chapter from the list on the left. Each chapter begins with a box containing a one-line recap of the chapter before, followed by the new chapter's introduction. The introduction explains how that part of the system works and why it matters. A short passage headed What the Slides Show then explains what the slides will add and in what order. The box fades as the slides begin to play on the map, with the full text displayed in the panel on the right.

Each slide picks up from the evidence before it and explains the significance of its figures alongside the facts. You can close any box using its ×. The controls at the bottom allow you to play or pause, move one slide forward or back, switch chapters, change the reading speed, show or hide the slide text, and see your position in the complete story.

Slides marked Regional Example show how a wider pattern appears in a particular country or region. Other slides compare every country for which a figure is published. Those countries are shaded according to the key, and hovering over one reveals its figure and year. One slide maps the largest flows of goods between pairs of countries. Lines are drawn so that none crosses the Pacific edge of the flat map, which means a line from China to the United States runs westward across Europe and the Atlantic; it shows that goods move between the two, not the route the ships take. Figures in these maps are calculated from the cited source data rather than entered individually by hand.

Why the Figures Can Be Trusted

Much of what this map says runs against what most people have been told about trade, and a careful reader should be sceptical. For that reason the map relies, as far as it can, on the system's own record-keepers. The figures come from the World Trade Organization, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the OECD and the statistical offices of the United Nations, from peer-reviewed studies, and from court documents in which companies have admitted the conduct described. Where a figure comes from a campaign organisation, the slide says so. Every slide carries a link to its source, and every documented record can be opened and checked.

The map also keeps to what the sources support. It does not say that trade has made nobody better off, or that every country would be richer behind closed borders. Several countries, mostly in East Asia, have grown rich partly by exporting, and Chapter 2 explains the conditions under which they did it. What the map does say is narrower and better documented: that the present rules were written mainly by and for the strongest economies and their largest companies, that the gains are divided very unequally, and that most of them go to the owners of a small number of firms.

What Is Drawn on Each Slide, and Why

Every slide includes a note headed On the Map. It explains which countries, organisations, lines and points appear, and why those locations were selected. The rule is consistent: a slide only draws places named in its own source. If a source provides a figure for every country, every country with a published figure is shaded. If the source names only a few examples from a much larger group, the note identifies them as examples. The map remains zoomed out far enough to show each location in its wider geographical context.

The Organisations, and Why These Ones

The map contains 220 organisations. World trade involves millions of companies and thousands of public bodies, so the directory cannot list every one. The selection uses a consistent test: is this organisation among the largest or most influential of its kind, globally or within its region, so that its decisions reach people well beyond its own premises?

That test is applied across several groups:

  • Rule-makers and international bodies: the World Trade Organization, the lenders, and the United Nations agencies that administer or measure trade.
  • Trade ministries and enforcers: the offices of the largest trading powers that negotiate deals and apply tariffs, sanctions and export controls.
  • Trade blocs and arbitration courts: the largest regional agreements, and the bodies under whose rules investors sue governments.
  • Banks, exchanges and payment systems: the main financiers of trade, the exchanges where commodity prices are set, and the networks payments pass through.
  • Export credit agencies: the 80 agencies on Trade Finance Global's published roster.
  • Trading houses, shipping lines, registries and canals: the largest in each field by volume handled.
  • Brands, retailers and manufacturers: companies that head the supply chains discussed in the story or hold a key stage in them.
  • Lobbies, think tanks, unions, researchers and watchdogs: the bodies that argue for the system and those that document it.
  • Investors and owners: the largest holders of shares across the companies above.

The legend includes a switch, Show Only the Largest of Each Kind. It hides the 79 smaller organisations included because the story names them or to complete a roster, such as the smaller export credit agencies. The directory is not a complete register of world trade. Inclusion means that an organisation is a significant part of the system; it is not, by itself, an allegation of wrongdoing.

Each organisation is placed in its headquarters city and coloured by category. Export credit agencies with a researched street address are placed at that address; the others are placed at the city level, as explained on their cards. Where several organisations share a city, their markers are arranged in a small ring so that each can be selected. Select an organisation to see what it does, what it owns or is owned by, and which chapters refer to it.

The Index and the Two Chapter Lists

The Index sits below the search box. It lists every organisation, every country named in the story and every documented record in alphabetical order. Beneath it are two lists of the same 22 chapters. The first follows the story from the top of the system down. The second, Find Your Region in the Story, groups chapters by the places where their slides are set.

Ports

The small dots are 3,630 seaports from the World Port Index, the list of the world's ports published by the United States National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. More than four fifths of traded goods by weight pass through ports like these. Larger ports are drawn slightly larger. Hover over a dot to see the port's name, country and size class.

How to Read It

Countries are shaded only while a slide is on screen. Most slides shade the countries their source names. The slides that compare every country shade each one by its published figure. When no story is playing, no country is shaded, because that shading would show where information has been collected rather than where an activity is actually taking place. A country not named in the story is therefore a gap in the research, not evidence that the pattern is absent.

An organisation's presence on the map means only that it is a significant part of world trade. The documented records inside the chapters provide the evidence for the claims made about particular actions or relationships. Each record carries a source link so readers can check the underlying material rather than relying on the map's description alone.

The Method section explains what qualifies as a chapter, how slides are sourced, how organisations and ports are placed, where the data comes from, and which parts of the subject remain unresearched.

What the Map Shows

The map has three main layers. The first is the story: how world trade is ruled, financed, carried and owned, told from the top of the system down. The second is the directory of major organisations in world trade, each placed at its headquarters. The third is the port layer, showing the seaports listed in the World Port Index. Documented records appear within the story as supporting evidence and can also be viewed separately.

What Counts as a Chapter

A chapter has to meet two tests. First, does it describe something that affects people beyond the location of one isolated event? The subject must help explain how trade works for people in many places. Second, does it show who rules, owns or is paid within the system? A fact about how much a country trades does not qualify on its own. It belongs in the story when it reveals how the system operates: who makes the decision, who bears the cost and who collects the gain.

A single court case, tariff or news report is not a chapter by itself. It can be included as evidence within a wider chapter when it helps demonstrate a recurring structure or pattern. The four bribery cases in Chapter 12, for example, are included together because four of the largest firms in one industry admitted the same conduct.

How the Story Is Ordered

The story opens with three chapters of foundation: how trade works, the history of the routes, and how the price of a product is divided today. It then follows the chain of authority from the top down. Part 2 covers the bodies that write the rules. Part 3 covers the currency and credit. Part 4 covers the firms that trade and carry the goods. Part 5 covers how production is divided and where profit is recorded. Part 6 covers what returns to the producing countries. Part 7 comes last because it closes the loop: the theory taught to officials is what leads them to administer the system, and the owners are where its earnings arrive.

This order is intended to make each layer understandable in the context of the one above it. Every chapter begins with an introduction to its subject and a short bridge explaining how the slides answer the chapter's question. Each slide then picks up from the evidence before it. A one-line recap appears at the top of the next chapter's box, so the reader carries the argument forward without a separate closing box after every chapter. The final chapter has no slides. It sets out the whole chain on one page.

How the Slides Are Built

Each slide is placed where the event or institution it describes is located and carries a source. If the slide is built around one of the map's documented records, it displays that record while the slide is playing. The text explains what a fact means immediately after presenting it, and translates large numbers into a scale readers can picture, such as cents in a dollar. These explanations are the map's interpretation of the evidence; the underlying figure is the source's.

Countries are highlighted in the colour associated with the role they play and remain highlighted until the chapter ends. Lines connect places between which goods, money, rules or ownership move. A line shows that a relationship or flow exists; it does not claim to show the exact route taken.

Where a slide names specific countries, only the countries identified by its source are highlighted, and the note beneath the slide explains the selection. Historical slides use present-day country outlines to show where events took place.

Slides That Cover Every Country

Global comparison slides use the latest figure each source publishes for each country from 2012 onward. The latest year therefore differs between countries and is shown in the country's tooltip. Every country with a published figure is shaded; no figures are adjusted or removed. The range is divided into five bands, shown in the map key.

Where the text names a typical rich or poor country, it is the median of the countries the World Bank classes as high-income or low-income among those with a figure. Some published figures look anomalous, such as Sudan's very low trade share or Bahrain's customs share for 2013. They are retained as published rather than silently corrected.

The datasets used for these comparisons are:

  • World Bank, World Development Indicators: each country's share of world goods exports (2025); trade as a share of national income; the current account balance; the average applied tariff, weighted by trade; customs and import duties as a share of tax revenue; debt service as a share of exports; and food as a share of goods imports. The Bank compiles these from the IMF, the WTO, UN Trade and Development and UN Comtrade.
  • Raw materials as a share of goods exports: calculated for this map by adding four World Bank series for the same year: fuels; ores and metals; food; and agricultural raw materials. The 60 per cent threshold mentioned in the text is the one UN Trade and Development uses to define commodity dependence. Its own measure is built slightly differently, so its count of dependent countries differs from the count given here.
  • OECD Trade in Value Added, 2023 edition: foreign value added as a share of gross exports in 2020, for the 76 economies the OECD publishes.
  • World Trade Organization: members and observers as listed on its website in November 2026. The membership count of 166 includes the European Union and customs territories that are not sovereign states and are not shaded separately.
  • World Bank, World Integrated Trade Solution: goods exports from each country to each partner.
  • World Trade Organization, Regional Trade Agreements database: the number of agreements in force that each country belongs to, as listed in November 2026.
  • UN Trade and Development, Investment Dispute Settlement Navigator: the number of known treaty-based claims brought against each country. The country figures shown are those the navigator listed when its total was 1,332, at the end of 2023; the total had reached 1,463 by the end of 2025. Countries listed with no claims are shaded in the lowest band.
  • Wier and Zucman, 2022 update of the Missing Profits estimates: corporate tax lost to profit shifting in 2019 as a share of corporate tax collected, calculated for this map by dividing the two columns of the authors' table for 45 countries. The worldwide figure of one trillion dollars in the text is the later estimate for 2022 from the same research group.
  • UN Trade and Development, World Investment Report 2019: the number of special economic zones in each region, shown as labelled points.

The slide Who Sells to Whom draws the 402 flows of at least 10 billion dollars. Those flows account for 70 per cent of the 22.5 trillion dollars of goods exports in the dataset. Showing all 26,375 recorded flows at world scale would make the map unreadable. Each country's tooltip gives its full totals in both directions. Figures are for 2022 where the country reported that year and otherwise for its latest year from 2019. For countries that did not report, their partners' import records are used instead.

How the Organisations Were Chosen and Placed

The About section explains the inclusion test: organisations are selected because they are among the largest or most influential of their kind, globally or within their region. Each is placed in its headquarters city. The export credit agencies come from Trade Finance Global's published roster and most are placed at their street address; the rest of the directory is placed at city level, as stated on each card.

When several organisations share a city, their markers are spread around a small circle so each can be selected. This changes only how the markers appear on screen; it does not alter their stored coordinates. Marker colours are adjusted against the basemap so they remain visible.

Organisation descriptions are intended to identify what each body is and which part of trade it affects. Where an organisation appears in the story, the relevant slide explains the action or relationship being discussed and provides the supporting source.

The Port Data

The port markers are the 3,630 ports of the World Port Index, Publication 150 of the United States National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, in its 2019 edition. The agency's own server could not be reached when this map was built, so the list was taken from a public copy of the index hosted on GitHub by Jordan Taylor. Only entries carrying a World Port Index number are drawn. A further 1,780 unnamed locations in that copy, which are not part of the index, were left out. The index classifies each harbour by size. The copy used here labels the classes major, minor, small and very small, and they are shown as given. It is a navigational reference, not a measure of trade volume, and a port's size class reflects its facilities, not the value of goods passing through.

Records

Each documented record is supported by at least one of the following: a court ruling or a guilty plea; an official inquiry or the report of an international organisation; a company's own filing or statement; a peer-reviewed study; or research by a named organisation based on primary material such as customs data. Where the source is a campaign organisation, the record names it. Estimates are described as estimates.

Coverage

The coverage estimates below are judgements, not measured counts. The first estimate, roughly 5 to 10 per cent, describes how much of the available evidence about who controls world trade has been gathered for this map. The second, roughly 30 to 45 per cent, estimates how much of the machinery behind an ordinary purchase the map can currently account for: the rules, the financing, the carriers, the traders, the chain of production and the ownership. The second estimate varies by region, as shown below.

These estimates describe the scope of the story and its records. They do not limit the global comparison slides, which use published figures covering most or nearly all countries regardless of how much the narrative has researched in each region.

What Was Left Out on Purpose

The map does not give separate chapters to how much each country trades, to forecasts of trade growth or to the day-to-day course of particular tariff disputes. Its subject is who controls trade and who is paid, not the trade statistics themselves. The world maps in Chapter 1 are included because the rest of the story cannot be followed without them.

The loan conditions attached by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, and the export credit agencies, are large subjects of their own. This map includes only what is needed to show where they sit in the chain.

What Is Missing

The map does not yet cover trade in services and data; the arms trade; trade in fish, timber and wildlife; the oil trade and how its price is set; migrant labour and remittances; the insurance and inspection industries; smuggling and the informal trade across land borders; or the trade agreements of China and the European Union one by one. These are gaps in the research, not evidence that the places or subjects concerned are unaffected.
